utterances.text: There were two wounded men that I helped. I brought one of them a shirt because he was bare chested. We could not help them, we could not carry them, and they stayed in that field wounded, two wounded men. Hurem and I went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender through this witness? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we have P65, the hand-drawn sketch of Bratunac; P66, the marked aerial photograph of Bratunac town; and P67, the picture of the digging machines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These documents are admitted into evidence. Are there any documents the Defence team would like to tender through this witness? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I was expecting Mr. Karnavas to respond. So the Defence would like to propose the following: That the sketch we used today be admitted into evidence, the one that we looked at together with the witness, and I did not hear whether it was D2/3 or D4/3. I didn't hear the number right, I think. But perhaps it was D4/3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it was D4/3. And by the way, we don't have that exhibit at all. Would you please furnish us with this document after the hearing. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is admitted into the evidence. Well, thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room, and we all wish you good luck in the future and a pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you have the next witness available here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And that will be -- there will be some protection, so if we could take a moment and prepare for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Good morning. I just wanted to make sure there's voice distortion as part of the protective measures with respect to this particular witness. I just wanted to advise Your Honour of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen a microphone is on there. Does it work? Maybe you could try it to see whether that microphone is working or not. Witness, would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Issa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the usher has a moment, I'm going to be asking you to look at a piece of paper and tell us by indicating yes or no if that is your name on this piece of paper, without saying your name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, I have to remind you that you have to turn off your microphone while the witness is answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'll try and remember that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, you are of Bosnian nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you are Muslim by faith. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that before the war, you were living with your family in Nova Kasaba. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you lived in a number of places, and in July of 1995 you were living in the village of Slapovici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We arrived there after the occupation of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and after Srebrenica we came to Slapovici. It's a village next to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where were you going to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I went to Srebrenica to school, the first year of secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand that in July of 1995, you were, in fact, 17 years old. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like you to think back to the 11th of July of 1995. Do you remember that day when the Bosnian Serb army overran the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, in fact, that didn't happen in a day, the beginning of July. There was shelling every day. One by one checkpoints were taken off the Dutch battalion. And in the end, we had to -- after the DutchBat left, we had to leave our location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, some people went towards Srebrenica, and some to the village of Suceska, we decided to go to the village of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you with at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I had a family. I had my mother, my three sisters, and my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where did your mother and sisters go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, we set off together with the village of Suceska, after which we separated. They went towards Potocari where the UN base was. And myself and my father, we went across the wood to the village of Jaglici where columns were established, and we set off in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you decide to go with your father in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: First of all, I wasn't certain -- I wasn't sure that UNPROFOR would protect us, certainly not the men, considering all the experience in the war and knowing what the Serb army had been doing. I decided to go with my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us about the degree of organisation of the column that was forming in the woods.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, it was in the meadows in front of the woods, on the 11th of July in the afternoon hours. There was a large number of people. They were predominantly men, young men, young boys. There were some women and children, but definitely a smaller number. Approximately there were 15.000 people, that's according to my estimate. Ten to 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how the column of 15.000 people were organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, that started before the dark, the columns were organised before the dark. And I stood with my father in -- we stood in a line. My father had been in the army, but that was more like a formality. He didn't have a uniform. He didn't have any weapons. During the attack on Srebrenica, he didn't go to any army position or line. He stayed with us. It was like a formality, and I decided to go with him. But as we got into the wood, the organising of the column lasted the whole night. And as we got into the woods, I saw soldiers, BH army soldiers who were preventing the civilians from going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you remain with your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: No. In that crowd of people, I was separated from my father, and I stayed alone for a while until I found my uncle. I found him by coincidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you seen your father since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I never saw my father again. I presume that he had gone ahead with the army, and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: There's something else. The organising of the column lasted almost all night, and it was already day when we wanted to get into the wood. Most civilians stayed behind. The soldiers went ahead. And I also saw some soldiers with the weapons that had remained behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened throughout the night and the day while you were in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We set off through the wood that morning. It was all calm. There was no shooting, nothing could be seen. And there was no firing on the column. We could hear some shooting in the distance but not on the column. We were in a line one by one. I didn't see ahead, I didn't see behind me how many people there were. It was a column going nonstop. After a while, the shelling started, the general shelling of the column started. There was shooting all over the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, I understand that on the 13th of July, you gave yourselves up to the Bosnian Serb army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But before that, there is something I have to say under which conditions we surrendered. On the 12th of July, we were shelled throughout the day. There were increasingly more injured people who were left in the woods. I can remember they were crying and screaming asking for help, but nobody was able to help them. And throughout the night there was firing on the column in the wood, and I also heard as we were running through the streams, through the brooks, I could hear the Serb soldiers shouting from the hills: "Balijas, where are you running? Why are you escaping? Come back." During that night, throughout the night, there was shelling, so in the morning we were still in the wood. And in the morning, I saw there were five or six people around me who were dead. And many people who were just walking around confused and scared. There were many wounded. I could see many people without legs, without arms, people without their stomach, people injured, people I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on the 13th of July after the heavy shelling throughout the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: That morning, at about 10.00 a.m., they started speaking over the loudspeakers. The Serb soldiers were saying we should surrender. They said: "Surrender or we'll shell you. You'll be taken according to all Geneva Conventions." That's exactly what was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the column surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: The column, in fact, the people were biding their time. And about 2.00 or 3.00, when those Serb soldiers gave their last warning that we should surrender or that we shall all be killed, that's when the column was organised. And they were going somewhere. We were in a wood. I couldn't see anything around me. The column was just going, we followed each other, and I followed everyone else. And there in the wood, according to my estimate, I saw 300 to 500 dead people. I had to cross those dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any soldiers upon surrendering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. Afterwards, as we left the wood, when I left, I saw that there were already people on the asphalt road and that the column had been arriving for some time. But when I got out, I saw the people were surrendering and that there were Serb soldiers around. In fact, I hadn't known that until I got there because it was a very long column. When I got closer to the bridge, in fact, we went over a bridge, there were about five Serb soldiers. I'm not quite sure. Five or six of them on that bridge. And they were saying that we should surrender, that we should hand over any weapons. If anybody had any bags, we should leave them, that we should hand over any gold or deutschmarks. That's when they insisted more than on other things on the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons at that point, anybody from the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see that. Many people - I forgot to say that - as we were going with a column, when we were going to surrender, many people who had had weapons, in fact very few people had had weapons. But many of those who had weapons, they just set off. They just left. I saw people just leaving the column. They did not want to go and surrender. I mean, those people who had weapons, they were lucky. They could just leave. Perhaps they survived later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you carrying anything with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I had a bag. I don't know what was in it. Some clothes, some food, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with that bag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, they were saying that we should leave it by the tank. There was a tank on the right-hand side. And we were just going to stand in lines on the road as we were arriving. And we also brought injured people from the wood, wounded people. We carried them with us. We were placing them in front of us. But many injured people were left behind. As I had already said, they were left to die there. Nobody was able to help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were lining up in lines along the road. Can you estimate the size of these lines and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Approximately about a hundred metre-long lines. I know there were five lines, five rows on one side of the road. According to my estimate, there were about a thousand, two thousand people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you saw the Serb soldiers upon arriving to the location where you surrendered. Can you describe how these Serb soldiers were dressed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Before I say that, I must say that they behaved very properly until everybody surrendered. They were not cursing. They were saying: "Come over here, nothing will happen to you" until everybody had surrendered and come out of the wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you are saying "they," you're referring to the Serb soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. However, when everybody surrendered, that's when they started to mistreat people. They, again, asked -- almost each one of them again asked for money. They were cursing, they were saying "Fuck your balija's mother." They were saying all kinds of things. I can't even remember what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how were these soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms on, multicoloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the colours that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were like olive drab, but with different shades of green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that you saw a tank that you were standing next to when the soldiers told you to put your bags down. Did you happen to notice anything about that tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: It was a tank, and there was some other armoured weapon, but I don't know what that was. It had machine-guns mounted on it, this other weapon. And then on the tank, I remember it was written "queen of death" in Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you at some point see any other soldiers or anybody else arrive aside from the soldiers you initially saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, let me just say something else. There were also soldiers who were standing there in front with their guns pointing at us. There were people with machine-guns. They had so many -- so much ammunition that ammunition belts were almost dragging on the ground. And after a while, two cars arrived. One was a police car, and one was a civilian vehicle, grey. And some soldiers arrived. They were sitting on the roof. And later on, I saw that they had different clothes on. In fact, they differed from police uniforms. They were also camouflage, but they had camouflage blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you at any point while there see any buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, there were some buses that were standing there. But these policemen who came, they and also some soldiers were asking for money. They were also cursing. And left from us, there were some buses that couldn't get through. I didn't know who or what this was about. I don't know who was on these buses. I later saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you later see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, the buses couldn't get through because of us, and one of the soldiers ordered that we should run along the road and carry the wounded. Throughout this time, we had to have our hands up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe how you had to have your hands up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Throughout the time while standing, we had to have our hands up above our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you were running down the road, were you instructed to do anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. As we were running along the road, Serb soldiers were running alongside us, and some of the men were carrying the wounded, and then we swapped. And those of us who were not carrying the wounded, one of the soldiers said "Come on, balijas, raise three fingers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the three fingers means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: That's a Serb sign, greeting. They cross themselves with three fingers. During the war, they stressed this so much that I didn't find it that important. But they wanted -- they wanted to show to those men on the bus what they were doing to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you at some point while running see the people on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I saw that these were people from Srebrenica, women, children. I saw some women and children crying. Many of them recognised their own children there, perhaps their husbands, too. I saw a school friend of mine, a girl who was on the bus -- who was on the truck as I was running.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular incident which you recall with one of the men as you were running that occurred between a Bosnian Serb soldier and one of the men from your column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't know where we were going, where we were running. Before we turned off into the meadow, on the road behind me, a Serb soldier asked someone: "In which unit were you in Srebrenica?" The man said: "I was in the unit" -- I don't know why. I don't know what this was about. I don't know why he said this, sort of firing unit or something like that. I don't know why he said it, out of defiance or something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when he said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Then the beating started. I heard blows behind me. I heard moans. He was probably hitting him with a rifle, but I didn't dare turn around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, you indicated you reached a meadow. Will you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. We turned left into the meadow. There were houses around, houses that had been destroyed. Some had been destroyed. Others not. Some had been torched. Trucks were still passing us by, and we were running -- on that side where we were running, I saw a man who lay there dead. We had to run around in order not to step on him. He was wearing civilian clothes. And I think he was an elderly person, and I think that he had been killed earlier on. Flies were attacking him, and as if there were some maggots on him. Then we turned into the meadow. There was high grass all around. Since this was a Muslim village, I knew from earlier on, from before, that there were Muslim houses there. We sat there. The grass was high. Nobody had cut it. But at the place where we came, the grass had been stepped on as if somebody had been there before. Perhaps some people were there before us, but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the meadow that you were in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, the grass was high. There were houses around. We all sat there. There was a tank there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you a map and ask you to point to us the direction that you left and the direction that you ended up in in this meadow, if you could, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: It's a small map, so it's hard to indicate this. Approximately this is where we surrendered, and we ran to Sandici, here on the left-hand side where we came to the meadow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the record, you're just pointing to a little bit below Sandici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: It's right over here. It's a small map. It's right here. Here where the triangle is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And while you have that map there, are you able to show us the direction that the buses were travelled from on the road when you saw the women and the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: The buses were going from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: And we were going in the opposite direction, towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, is this a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Sorry, certainly, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we are going to have a break. So please remain where you are until the usher shows out of the courtroom. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, sir, you were telling us that you at some point gathered in the Sandici meadow or near the Sandici meadow. Can you tell us how many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Approximately 2.000. All the men who were over there came, came to the meadow, I mean. But I don't know whether there were any people out there before that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And after you gathered in the meadow, what happened there at that meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, as we came there, we sat down one by one. We were all facing the asphalt road where the tank was. And in front of it was a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that Serb soldier doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: He started saying things. I remember some of it, but I didn't listen to most of it because I wasn't really interested. Actually, I wasn't really up to it. I felt depressed, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall some of the things he was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Before that, I'll tell you what he looked like. He had a black scarf on his head. He was tall, corpulent. He had a uniform, a camouflage uniform, too. A multicoloured one, one piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember the -- you say multicoloured. Do you remember if there was a particular colour that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, these are shades of green, camouflage uniform that the army of Republika Srpska wore. Later on, I saw it on television, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us what he said to the crowd.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: He talked a lot. But I remember some of the things he said. "Where were you wounded? Why didn't you surrender earlier? If they had surrendered earlier, they would not have been there now." He asked whether there was anybody who was a medical person to dress the wounds of your wounded, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anybody, a medical person there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I didn't see. But one of the men got up, got up, and he started searching him, frisking him. I don't know why. And he had pointed a gun at him. He was using one hand to search him and the other -- and in the other hand, he held his gun pointed at him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this man at some point dress the wounds of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I don't know what happened later to the man. I just remember that, when he searched him. I don't know. I can't remember now whether he did dress anybody's wounds. I didn't see that. I don't know. My head was down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Another thing, this soldier who was saying all those things previously, he said that we would be taken to Bratunac, to some hangars, and that we would be exchanged when our authorities asked for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did -- do you remember if anything was said about any of the boys that were in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Let me just say something else. He was saying something, and I remember when he said "We are from Serbia." I don't know why he said that, but I just heard him say this. "We are from Serbia. We will be here, guard you." Later on, another unit came that took over from them, and he said: "Now, these other guys would come in. They're nice. They're not going to do anything to you." He said that in Bratunac, there will be no dinner for us. He said it sort of a bit ironically because we didn't really feel like dinner or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember if anything was said about the -- about anybody in particular in that crowd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: He said this a bit ironically. He probably knew what would happen to us later. Of course we wouldn't need any dinner. After that -- actually, trucks were still passing down the road, and buses too. He said that whoever was born in 1980 or who was even younger than that could get up and go on to the bus. Three boys reported, I believe. And they left. I knew one of them. He was older, but he was just short, so he looked a lot younger. He raised his hand. He reported to them and left. After that, another child, perhaps 12 or 13, or perhaps even younger, raised his hand, and he said: "No, no, not possible. You're staying behind." I was there with my uncle. He was also making me raise my hand, but I didn't dare to. I was older, too, and I didn't dare since he had told the child that he couldn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what time this was during the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hearing the translation, not the English. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, approximately what time did this soldier address the crowd in the Sandici meadow?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's a technical problem. I can't hear the English translation and it appears the interpreters are unable to hear the witness for the translation into English from the witness. So perhaps we can just deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I hope the interpreters will check the buttons, because we hear not English on that channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English interpretation on this channel? This is the channel that has been used throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I can now hear, Your Honour, without hearing the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, I think we still have the wrong channel. Shall I try that again. Yes, it seems okay. Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, approximately what time did this soldier address the crowd in Sandici? Are you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: [In English] It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is unable to hear the translation. I think we're still experiencing technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, would you please say something into the mic so we can check whether it's okay or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear a thing. I can only hear English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us approximately what time was it when the Serbian soldier addressed the crowd in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, sometime around 5.00. I can't say for sure, but around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier, sir, you mentioned that you were told that you would be taken to Bratunac to a hangar. Can you tell us if at some point did that occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Before I say that, I have something else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt, and I do this with a great deal of hesitation. However, this particular witness has repeatedly failed and refuses to answer direct questions given to him. I understand he wishes to provide lots of information. He could do so through the questioning of the Prosecution rather than volunteering information and not being responsive to the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I think you have to answer the question put to you by the Prosecution first. If you want to add something, please feel free to do so after you answer the question by the Prosecution. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. But I do have to say something. If I were only to answer in a single sentence, it wouldn't sound convincing at all. I cannot simply skip over facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. But you have to answer the question first, and later on -- and after that, you may add something to your answer, say, give some explanations. I think this is the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this technical error, I hadn't even finished the answer I was giving.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, that was my fault in the sense that I may have been distracted by that error, and I'll go back to that question, and that may resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir, just going back to when you were gathered in the Sandici meadow, you told us that you were -- the soldier addressed the crowd, indicated to us what he had said. Is there anything else that occurred at Sandici while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is something that I think is important. After this other unit came, those who had surrounded us, and we had been surrounded before that, too, we were ordered to lie down, to lie on our stomachs. That is to say, facing the ground. To put our hands above our necks and to applaud and to say, all of us together in unison "Long live the king, long live Serbia." We were there for about three hours lying that way. We didn't dare raise our heads. Shooting started near us, but I couldn't see that. I couldn't see anything until later, until I got up. Perhaps, perhaps around dusk, we were told that we could get up. And when I got up, I saw a Serb soldier shooting at a house from the outside. This was a burst of gunfire. I couldn't see what was in the house, but what I can say is that my uncle told me that there was a man whom we knew and who is no longer there. After that, I didn't see any wounded. They were probably taken into that house and killed. I don't know what happened to them. Anyway, as we were running, they went on the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And after you were instructed to get up, were you -- what were you told to do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We were told that we would be going to Bratunac. Five or six lorries arrived, large, articulated lorries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We were ordered to get on those lorries, and I was in the last lorry. They were covered with tarpaulin cover, only the last part wasn't covered but the side was closed. And we had to run along, and then catch the side in order to climb up on the lorry. Many people couldn't get up on there. Some of them were hit because as soon as somebody would get hold of the side, then the other man would also be forced to get hold of the side, and then people were falling over each other. So it was very difficult to climb on the lorry. And then when one lorry load was loaded, people were saying that there was no more room, yet more people were loaded on. They were jamming people together, so we were standing like sardines. We were standing up. We couldn't sit down. There was no room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the size of the lorry that you were loaded on to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: The lorry didn't have a trailer, but it was a long lorry. It was the longest transport lorry there was. It probably could have carried some 20 tonnes, according to my estimate. It's just the largest type of lorries. It didn't have a trailer, but it was very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were in the lorry with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, 100 to 200 people. Perhaps even more. Considering that we were literally on top of each other. That we actually would fall off each other. And then there's something else. Behind us, there was a Golf car that was driving, soldiers, and we were told that we mustn't jump off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some point get to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We arrived, and we -- by the time we were loaded on the lorry, it was already night, and we arrived in Bratunac at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Through that last part of the lorry, I saw that we were somewhere in town, in Bratunac. In fact, I saw lights on the buildings. I saw we had gone through the town, and we were put somewhere. But I don't know where that was. In fact, the lorry just stopped somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long had they stopped for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Because my lorry was the last one in this convoy, when I say that it stopped, what I mean is it just stopped somewhere in town when we arrived in Bratunac. And we stayed there the whole night. And we asked for water, and the Serb soldier just swore at me. They were saying "quiet," cursing our balija's mother, hitting the sides of the lorry. The rifle -- I presume it was a rifle butt because there was quite a strong echo we could hear. I only know that I couldn't feel anything. We were so pressed together. We were so jammed together that I couldn't feel anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions inside the truck with you jammed together.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: It was unbearable. It was hell. As we were driving, and then we stopped, then we just fell over each other. As I told you, I couldn't feel anything. My body had gone dead. My legs had no feeling. I was numb. I was feeling numb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the next morning on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: The next morning, the lorry set off, and I saw, and the other people were saying, that lorry was leaving Bratunac. I was able to see at the crossroads at the red light that there were more lorries in front of us. Some people were saying that they had seen an UNPROFOR APC, but I hadn't seen it. And lorries were riding until the exit out of Bratunac, and then they stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when your lorry stopped at the exit of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, we were on this lorry. We were sitting, lying on top of each other. We asked for water. We were very thirsty. We were given one sip of water, but that was nothing. It was like just a drop. People were dying to get some water. At one moment, I tried to get up to see what was behind. There was a part of the lorry that was uncovered. And when I got up, I saw a bus full of people. But the driver was sitting, and his rifle was leaning against the windshield. So when I got up to see, he then pointed the rifle at me telling me to get down. Through the hole on the tarpaulin cover, I saw that there had been a garden by the road, and a house, and there were several Serb soldiers standing there. There were some civilians, children were riding on their bicycles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier, sir, that as you were leaving Bratunac, you saw other lorries. Did you notice who was in those lorries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: That bus behind us, people were all jammed together. I didn't recognise anyone, but they were probably the people who would end up with us later. And there were also people who were on the lorries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether those people were men or women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How long were you in the lorry outside of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: For some two to three hours, perhaps maybe until 10 to 10.00 or later than that perhaps. But it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your lorry start to move at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. Before the lorry set off, one of the soldiers came and closed the end part of the tarpaulin cover and said that he's closing this cover for our own safety. And then lorries continued to drive in the direction of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although the cover was closed, were you able to see anything on the outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, through this hole that I was observing through, I could see that we were going through Konjevic Polje, that we were on our way to Zvornik, Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you at some point come to a stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We stopped. Once we had gone past Zvornik, I didn't know where we were going, and people were saying -- probably they were also observing through some kind of holes. They said we had turned off somewhere towards Tuzla, but in any case, we didn't turn off towards Bijeljina because we were all thinking that we were going somewhere to a camp, like Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you to look at the same map that you looked at earlier and to show us the route that you took from Bratunac and where you eventually ended up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We went along this road.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone please be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the Drina River. By the Drina River, Zvornik, Karakaj, and we turned left. I didn't know where we turned off, but I found out later. And we arrived there. I don't know the name of that place. I mean, I did not know at that time. I saw through the hole in the canvas the emptied lorries. I saw that there was a building. It is only later that I would find out that it was a school, once we actually entered this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, earlier you pointed to a spot near Petkovci. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecutor is testifying right now. The witness has never mentioned that name, and I think it needs to come from the mouth of the witness, not the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, if you want to confirm something, put it in the form of a question and address it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I was just indicating what he was indicating for the purposes of the record. I certainly wasn't testifying, but I will bear that in mind for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us how long did you remain in the truck when you arrived at that location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We remained there for about an hour. There were several lorries around us, and buses as well. I saw that the buses were empty. It was some kind of a concrete playing field. The conditions inside the lorries were unbearable. We were shouting and screaming for water and to be let out. If I can just say what the conditions were, one of the people -- one of the men, he was drinking his own urine. That's how thirsty we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody give you any water while you were in that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: No. No, nobody gave us water there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time was it when you finally got off that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I can't quite recall the time. But it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how the Bosnian Serb soldiers were dressed when you got off the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: The same clothes as I'd described before. But you have to understand that my head was bent down, so I was not able to observe many things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened to you after you got off the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Some of the soldiers were cursing mother, saying: "See, we are driving you. You wouldn't drive us." And then we were going one after each other into this building down the steps, into this building that I found out later was a school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you to look at a photograph, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Exhibit P14.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that photograph on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recognise that building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. That was this building that we were in. That's the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you indicated that you went into this school up some stairs. I'm going to ask you to look at another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep interrupting, but Ms. Issa is leading the witness. He never testified that he went up some stairs or went in the school yet. If she would like to get those answers, she needs to ask the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a right objection. Rephrase your question, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, you can tell us what happened when you entered the school or where you went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I think it's a mistake. First, we went down the steps to get in front of the school building. And once we got into the building, then we went up the stairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm going --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I have something else to add. As we were going down the steps, one of the Serb soldiers was standing in front of the door. And he took a rifle by the barrel, and he hit everybody across their backs. But because he couldn't get everybody, one of the people from the middle of the stairs stopped the line of us going in and started sending us through one by one in front of the door so that then each one of us would bend down and be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a particular incident at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. A man who was in front of me, a Serb soldier asked him: "Do you know me?" And this man answered: "I know, brother. I do, brother." And the Serb soldier, as he was holding this rifle, he hit him in the stomach and he started beating him up and saying "Who do you know?" As if this man wasn't supposed to know him. After that, there was a pause because of this man. And then I got in without being beaten. Perhaps I was looking young. Perhaps they felt sorry, but I didn't get beaten. As I -- as we were getting in, we went to the right-hand side up the stairs. One of the Serb soldiers asked whose land is this? We kept quiet, and he said: "This is Serbian land and will always remain so." And we had to repeat this after him. Again, he asked: "Whose is Srebrenica?" And he then replied: "Srebrenica has always been Serbian and will continue to be that." And we had to repeat this as we went up the stairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you went up the stairs, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We followed a corridor to the left. I don't know how many, but there were about maybe four or five classrooms where there was a noise of the people that could be heard coming from the classrooms, of the people who were already inside. I had gotten into the last one or the one before last. I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask you to look at the photograph that's on your screen, and then another photograph, and ask you if you recognise the image that's on your screen at this point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. That is the inside of the building. Those are the stairs that I remember. This is where we went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you can look at the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's P14.4. Can you tell us, sir, what that image depicts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: This is the corridor that we went through that was upstairs on the first floor. That was on the floor -- the first floor of the school. These are the classrooms, and I think I may have gone into this last classroom. I can't quite remember, but I think that was the last classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the door furthest to the left of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, the door which is on the right-hand side of the wall, furthest one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record, the previous photograph, Your Honour, was already marked as Prosecution Exhibit 14.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us how many men were in the classroom with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I can't remember quite how many. But I know that the classroom was overcrowded. There were even more people than on the lorries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions inside that classroom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: The conditions were very difficult. We were very thirsty. People couldn't go to the toilet. Almost everyone was soaked with urine. I was soaked with urine. Soaked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any water at any point while you were in the classroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Later on, while we were still there, we were given some. But very little, just a drop. One of the men got out and gave us some water, and I think we just got a drop. We just opened our mouths to receive that drop of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, what was the air like in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: It was very stuffy, very stuffy. We couldn't breathe. Even in the truck, when the temperature was so high outside and when the tarpaulin was closed, in the classroom, it was even worse because there were a lot more of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any windows in the classroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. There were some windows. When I was coming, I saw that there was even an asphalt road below the school. And once, somebody tried to open the window. Many people were screaming, asking for water. When somebody tried to open the window, all of a sudden, a burst of gunfire followed. I know that all of the glass panes broke and fell. There were five or six men who were wounded by the glass. And I also think that it was due to the ammunition, too. I know that there was this one person who was wounded in the neck and who screamed real bad. One of the soldiers, one of the Serb soldiers, came to the door and again asked for money. Some men gave some money that they had hidden before that. They didn't give it before that. They probably thought that they would survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after they gave their money to the soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Nothing happened. He took the money and left. But later, since we were clamouring, asking for water, we were thirsty, he came to caution us. He said: "Quiet, quiet." And then he pointed at two young men and said that they were responsible for us. If we were noisy, then they would be killed. The man begged us to keep quiet, but nobody kept quiet. We were very thirsty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a Serb soldier at some point ask for any men from certain places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes. Once he walked in and said: "Is there anyone here from Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Glogova, Osmice, and he mentioned some other villages. I can't remember all of them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the men respond?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Yes, some men raised their hands and said "There's us." He told them to come out, and they did. And I heard beating and moaning in the hallway. They didn't return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that evening of 14 July when darkness fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, when darkness fell, shooting started around the school. Judging by the reverberations in the hallway, it went on all the time. I heard some of the soldiers in the hallway speaking probably from one of the classrooms. He would say: "Come out, out you go" two or three at a time, or five. "Come on, out you go balijas." And so on. And then bursts of gunfire would be heard every time, every time when these men managed to get downstairs, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did this carry on, until what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: This lasted until about midnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Then somebody came and said that it was our turn, that we would be going out later for some kind of examination. I don't know what kind of examination this was. He was saying something, but I cannot remember all of it now. He mentioned something about an exchange, too, but I cannot recall these details now. At any rate, we were supposed to go out for some kind of an examination. Before that, people were talking amongst themselves, and it was clear to us that they were killing people from the other classrooms, that it would be better for us if we all ran out at the same time. They couldn't kill everyone. Because there were many more of us in comparison with the soldiers, although they had weapons. Many people didn't want to do that. They said: "Well, maybe we'll survive. We shouldn't run out." Nobody wanted to die.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you were ordered to come out of the classroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: My uncle was there with me in the classroom, and I asked him whether we should go out together. Another man gave me some clothes because I was soaked in urine, and he gave me his T-shirt, and I put it on. And I asked my uncle whether we should go out together, and he said that we should not go out together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen your uncle since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go out of the classroom with anyone, or were you on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: I went out with a man. I don't know who he was. When I got out in front of the classroom, there was a Serb soldier who ordered us to take off our clothes down to the waist and to take off our shoes. I only had socks on my feet. I didn't have any footwear. He said that I should take that off, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do after you removed your clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: After that, he tied our hands on our backs. I don't know what was used. It wasn't a wire, but it was some kind of thread that was very sharp. And it felt most uncomfortable on the wrists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after tying your hands together, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: We were pushed into another classroom, another classroom where it was dark. There was no light. There were other men around me, also tied up, with their clothes off. One could discern footwear, and I was walking on the shoes of people who had probably been there before us, who had been taken out before we were taken out. There's one thing I have to say. When I was in the classroom, in the classroom where I was, I saw a blackboard, and I assumed that this was a school. Later on, I found out that it was, indeed, a school, and I found out where we were. But then, I didn't know where we had been. They drove us there, and I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, sir, how long you remained in that second classroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-111
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but until everybody was tied up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks like we only have a few minutes left, and perhaps this might be a good time to take the break and continue the evidence tomorrow subject, of course, to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, I'm afraid you have to stay here for another night. During your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody about your testimony, and do not let anybody talk to you about it. And when the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. There's an announcement I have to make. That is, there's some changes in the scheduling. On Wednesday, we'll have the afternoon session instead of the morning session. Well, I think that's all. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.
